In addition, multiple 22 DCX STRATEGY objectives for new materials are to decrease the sensitivity of mechanical properties to heat treatments while increasing the strength and toughness relative to HSLA-100. Achieving these objectives will provide the following benefits: • Enhanced vessel HE load limits and capabilities • Increased vessel design flexibility (section thickness, weld design, tolerances) • Reduced forming, forging, and fabrication challenges (delamination, defects, heat treatment) Preliminary material comparisons have identified materi- als to investigate further. For forgings this includes SA-508, Grade 4N, Class 2, and SA-541. For plate material and heads this includes SA-517, SuperElso 690, and SA-543. These have comparable strength to HSLA-100, but all have much low- er ductility. Studies on these materials will be required to evaluate their ability to replace HSLA-100. Inside the vessel, advanced fragment mitigation materials such as aerogels, B4C, Gigacreet, and/or Dynema/Spectra will be evaluated to enhance VCS performance. In addition to vessel materials, design changes will be investi- gated to advance VCS designs from known leak paths/mech- anisms and increase the HE load limit for a 6 ft. vessel. The DACS vessel has a 2.5 in. nominal wall thickness. Improved mechanical properties and/or a greater wall thickness will be required to realize higher HE load limits, which would expand the programmatic value and range of experiments possible at DARHT. To support near-term program requirements for larger HE loads and increased device sizes, two existing HSLA-100 8 ft. vessels are being evaluated for use. These 8 ft. diameter, 2.5 in. thick wall vessels were constructed in the early 1990s as the first vessel design for DARHT. The vessels were fabricated using HSLA-100, but the 8 ft. design did not move past the construction of these two vessels and a complete VCS (vessel weldment, covers, windows, furniture, armor, etc.) was never realized. One of the two 8 ft. vessels was used for the remediation of Manhattan Project–era artillery shells that were radiologically contaminated; it is unclear if it remains usable for hydrodynamic experiments. A comprehensive inspection and fitness-for-service evaluation will be conducted to determine the path forward for this vessel. The second 8 ft. vessel has been sitting outside, due to a lack of indoor heated storage space, and has weathered significantly. It is in the process of being refurbished and inspected to obtain a baseline condition for the vessel weldment.
